This thesis deals with the automatic classification of the top three leading causes of

preventable blindness namely Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD), Glaucoma, and

Diabetic Retinopathy (DR). The work endeavors to overcome the existing architecture

limitations which result in inter-class feature interference and failure in important severity

grades due to systematic issues and therefore proposes a Bio-Inspired Hierarchical Gating

Multi-Expert Fusion system (HG-MEF-Bio) that endeavors to obtain specialist-level

accuracy at a single inference, outputting a single eleven-class output. A methodology

based on an expert-then-fuse paradigm utilizing three benchmark datasets namely

EyePACS for DR, AMDNet for AMD and ORIGA for Glaucoma, with approximately

22,700 fundus images was devised. Three specific disease classification models

trained using hybrid architectures (ResNet-50, ViT-B/16, and EfficientNet-B4) that are

embedded within several bio-inspired algorithms such as the Firefly Algorithm, Genetic

Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimisation, Artificial Bee Colony, Differential Evolution and

Grey Wolf Optimiser ensuring clinical reliability with the implementation of a

differentiable Expected Calibration Error (ECE) loss.

The proposed system achieved an

expert model accuracy of 97.25% for AMD, 95.45% for Glaucoma and 93.6% for DR

while improving the detection of Severe DR class by 39.3%-92.8%. The HG-MEF-Bio

model obtained a validation accuracy and macro-F1 score of 95.14% and 0.9278

respectively and outperforming current state-of-the-art. This thesis is one of the first few

approaches which implement a combination of different bio-inspired algorithms within a

training loop to perform classification of retinal images. Future works include clinical

In terms of human performance, vision is the modality which conveys more information,

as the visual system is thought to transmit 80% of all incoming data from the external

environment to the brain. Vision is a key component of virtually all facets of human

functionality, social life and quality of life.

Since early on it was clear to the international

community that blindness or partial sight deficiency is among the most debilitating and

economically costly public health problems of the 21st century. However the problem is

growing at an exponential rate. In a recent World Health Organization (WHO) estimate,

about 2.2 billion people around the world live with vision impairment or blindness, almost

half of these being cases that were preventable or have not been properly addressed. The

impact of visual impairment is uneven, with over 90% of those visually disabled globally

living in low- and middle- income countries (LMICs). Available care to address the issue

is significantly limited due to lack of medical professionals trained in the diagnosis and

management of ophthalmic diseases, available technology and limited resources in these

LMICs.

The highest proportion of world's blind people reside in sub-Saharan Africa and

South and Southeast Asia where the disease is predominantly due to a retina condition and

they also harbor the largest percentage of the worlds hypertensive and diabetic population. Retina disease are also the biggest reason for worldwide blindness. Refractive errors,

conversely, can be corrected by the prescription of corrective lenses. Retinal conditions

affect the neuronal components of the eye where the light energy is transformed into

electrical signals to be processed by the brain, through a network of light sensitive

photoreceptor cells, pigment epithelium and retina ganglion cells together with supplying

blood vessels, that have sustained a damage and, in most cases, permanently. In relation to

this therapy window of damage and the criticality to the moment in which the therapy is

administered is extremely narrow, that the three retinal diseases objects of this work (AMD,

Glaucoma, and Diabetic Retinopathy) comprises the majority of preventable blindness

The International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness (IAPB) estimates that the number

of people living with moderate-to-severe visual impairment will rise to an estimated 474

million by 2050, while the number of blind people will reach 61 million. This is due to

population ageing and the rising prevalence of metabolic disorders including diabetes and

hypertension. And it's also damaging to our wallets - vision impairment results in USD 411

billion loss in global productivity every year (excluding all the emotional and societal cost

paid by people with visual impairment and their careers).

The human retina is a delicate tissue layer on the inner posterior wall of the eye (diameter

approx 42mm, thickness 0.5mm) and has in the order of 120 million photoreceptors (rods

and cones) in addition to numerous bipolar, amacrine, horizontal and retinal ganglion cells

that manage the early processing of retinal data. The center of the retina (macula) supports

fine central vision, has a high concentration of cone photoreceptors and contains the fovea. Approximately 15 degrees nasally to the macula is the optic disc, where the retinal ganglion

cell axons converge to form the optic nerve and transmit visual information to the brain. It

is because of the composition of the retina and the resulting unique distribution of changes

that are used for diagnosis of AMD, glaucoma and DR, that each disease has a different

profile and pattern of change evident in the imaging modality for each research project;

AMD is a progressive, chronic and degenerative disease of the macula that affects more

than 50 years old people.

There are two types of AMD. The most common one is Dry AMD (geographic atropy)

which accounts for 85-90% of the AMD cases, characterized by soft and confluent drusen

and an atropy of RPE, while Wet AMD (neovascular AMD) accounts for the 10-15% cases,

and is responsible for about 90% of severe vision loss associated with AMD, is due to sub-

RPE neovascular membrane that leak, proliferate and bleed, leading to retinal edema,

haemorrhages and rapid photoreceptor death, and which can be stabilized or partially

reverted by anti-VEGF therapy when the disease is at its earlier stages.

text:
When visualized on a fundus photograph, AMD presents several signs: hard and soft

drusen (yellowish spots, small and large with sharp/blurry borders), zones of

hypopigmentation and hyperpigmentation of the RPE, areas of geographic atrophy, and in

wet AMD the presence of fluid or haemorrhage under the retina, as well as neovascular

membranes. The fact that AMD has a complex and various aspect on fundus image in

different types and stages made it a challenging classification object for automatic system. Glaucoma is the most common cause of irreversible blindness in the world and has afflicted

approximately 76 million individuals currently, with the figure predicted to increase to

more than 111 million by the year 2040. The principal difference to AMD is that whilst

central vision is impaired with AMD, glaucoma causes progressive neuronal cell death in

the RGCs and subsequent axonal degeneration, yielding characteristic patterns of visual

field loss that initially occur at the peripheral periphery of vision and often goes unnoticed

until a great amount of the nervous system has been affected.

Standard clinical screening for retinal diseases necessitates examination of fundus photos

or slit lamp biomicroscopic examination by a human ophthalmologist or optometrist skilled

in retinal diseases. While a human specialist provides highly accurate diagnoses when

expertly employed, it is limited by a series of structural problems which prevents the ability

to scale, access and standardize diagnoses on a population level:

Firstly, the total number of ophthalmologists in the world is hopelessly undersubscribed

relative to need, particularly in LMICs.

classify these features. The system in general works very well on lab data (good sensitivity

and specificity for some types of lesion in controlled conditions) but has terrible

performance for clinical images (due to variations in illumination, image quality, camera

imaging modality or disease category. New imaging modality or disease classification

requires new features to be manually engineered by experts. This makes the CADe system

image analysis.

With the demonstration by LeCun et al. On hierarchical feature extraction

using convolutional layers and the development of large labelled datasets and GPUs, it has

become possible to build diagnostic systems that can learn relevant features directly from

images. The era of deep learning in ophthalmic AI began when Gulshan et al. Showed in

Nature in 2016 that a deep CNN model, when trained on 128,175 retinal images, achieved

comparable sensitivity and specificity on DR detection to the median ophthalmologist. The

last few years have witnessed a surge of deep learning methods applied to retinal disease

classification. Among these, various CNN architectures (VGGNet, ResNet, DenseNet,

InceptionNet, EfficientNet, MobileNet, etc.) and ensembled methods are developed. These

methods are shown to have strong performance in disease classification, forming the basis

for more complicated multi-disease and multi-expert frameworks such as the Hierarchical

Gating Multi-Expert Fusion (HG-MEF) proposed in this thesis.

The principal bio-inspired algorithms leveraged in the present work encompass six distinct

algorithmic paradigms, each modelling a different natural phenomenon. The Genetic

Algorithm (GA), inspired by Darwinian natural selection, evolves populations of candidate

solutions (chromosomes) through selection, crossover, and mutation operations, and is

employed in this work to adaptively evolve per-class loss function weights during training. The Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO) algorithm, inspired by the collective movement

patterns of bird flocks and fish schools, updates a swarm of candidate solutions according

to individual and collective best positions, and is employed to optimise per-class decision

thresholds both during and after training. The Firefly Algorithm (FA), inspired by the

bioluminescent signalling behaviour of fireflies, updates agent positions based on relative

brightness (fitness), and is integrated with Grad-CAM saliency to guide EfficientNet-B4

The Grey Wolf Optimiser (GWO) simulates the hierarchical hunting behaviour of grey

wolf packs — with alpha, beta, and delta wolves guiding the search — and is deployed to

optimise multi-way cross-attention blend weights in the expert fusion layers. The Artificial

Bee Colony (ABC) algorithm, modelling the foraging behaviour of honeybee colonies

through Employed, Onlooker, and Scout bee phases, is applied to optimise the routing bias

in the fusion gating network. Finally, Differential Evolution (DE), a gradient-free

continuous optimiser that generates new candidate vectors through differential mutation,

is applied to optimise per-expert feature scaling factors in the fusion feature mixing

module. Together, these six algorithms constitute an unprecedented ensemble of bio-

inspired intelligence woven throughout every level of the proposed system.

text:
Most current automated retinal disease systems are disease-specific: either classifying DR

alone, or AMD alone, or Glaucoma alone, being trained and tested on samples held out

from the same distribution, and tested on data which originates from the same disease-

specific dataset. Whilst these single-disease systems perform well within their given scope,

they do not reflect the reality of clinical screening: a given patient could be afflicted with

multiple retinal conditions simultaneously; it is desired that all screening must start from

the same fundus camera/screening visit and perform triage across all diseases. To overcome these shortcomings, several multi-disease approaches have been proposed,

where systems are trained to perform multiple tasks simultaneously. When a single deep

neural network is trained to perform multiple classification tasks at the same time, then

there is a possibility of inter-class interference of feature representations: The

representations learnt for AMD classification may be counter-productive for DR grading

in the latter layers of the network, where discrimination is based upon subtle patterns in

retinal images.

The Hierarchical Gating Multi-Expert Fusion (HG-MEF) architecture proposed in this

thesis addresses this challenge through an expert-then-fuse paradigm: three disease-

specific expert models are independently trained on their respective disease datasets,

developing specialised and maximally discriminative feature representations for each

condition, before being unified through a learned hierarchical fusion network. This

architecture preserves the benefits of disease-specific specialisation whilst enabling cross-

disease interaction through the fusion layer's cross-attention mechanism — producing a

system that is both more accurate at the individual disease level and more clinically

The main problem that the current thesis addresses is that how to build a clinically

dependable, scalable and explainable automated classifier for the top three human causes

of blindness (Age-Related Macular Degeneration, Glaucoma, Diabetic Retinopathy) on

fundus photographies under a unified multi-disease model while escaping from the

structural limitations of both single-disease model and naïve multi-disease model. While it has been witnessed with numerous progresses in deep learning based ophthalmic

AI, there remains a large and clinical-meaningful gap between capabilities of current

automated models and the practical needs of reliable clinical deployment for ophthalmic

screening programs. This disconnect exists across five correlated factors, each of which is

targeted by an architectural feature of the HG-MEF and HG-MEF-Bio models developed.
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text:
Currently, multiple-disease classification methods typically use one generic deep neural

network trained concurrently for all disease classes. Though efficient from the computation

aspect, it inherently has an optimisation problem where network should be optimized with

features representations of AMD (macular drusen and RPE changes) Glaucoma (optic disc

shape and RNFL features) and DR at 5 grades (microaneurysms, hemorrhages,

neovascularisation). Anatomical location, lesion morphology and scale of relevant features

differ drastically between these three diseases, and gradients from different supervision

objectives mutually cancel out each other during backpropagation. The outcome is that no

one disease achieves good performance as all models compromise their optimisation

This issue was directly witnessed in Phase-I of this project, where a generic ViT trained

simultaneously for all diseases attained only around 90-91% average accuracy and

performed particularly badly on the minority DR severity grades (Glaucoma: 78%

accuracy, DR mild: recall far below clinical standards). Individual disease training experts

for each disease as proved for architecture 1 baseline on Phase-II can address this inter-

class conflict by having accuracy 97.75% for AMD, 94.4% for Glaucoma, 86.8% for DR.
section_heading: 1.2.2 Gap I — Inter-Class Feature Interference in Unified Models

text:
Class imbalance is inherent in retinal disease screening data-sets because in any unselected

population-level screening cohort most subjects are normal or have early mild stages of

disease, whereas clinically significant stages (Severe DR, Proliferative DR) are rare.This

characteristic distributional skewness causes systematic training failure: normal cross-

entropy loss functions are dominated by the contribution of majority classes to the gradient,

resulting in decision boundaries that trivialize towards majority class classification yielding

high aggregate accuracy at the expense of failure on rare but clinically relevant minority

The clinical failure illustrated by the Phase-I and Architecture 1 results were 86.8 percent

aggregated DR detection, but only 39.3 percent correctly classified Severe DR (most

clinically relevant acuity). The screening system that this fails as such fails to detect >60%

patients needing immediate laser photocoagulation or anti-VEGF therapy for Proliferative

DR and blindness. Remedies such as class-weighted cross-entropy, over-sampling, and

data augmentation have proved inadequate, and the three algorithmic solutions for the

training failure (SOL1, SOL2, SOL3) developed for Architecture 2, Phase-II push the

accuracy for Severe DR to 92.8 percent (a gain of 53.5 percentage points).
section_heading: 1.2.3 Gap II — Critical Minority Class Failure Under Real-World Class Imbalance

text:
Although hybrid models have a clear tendency to perform better than single trained models

on medical image classification, the current methodology for ensemble methods relies

upon static fusion, that is, average and majority vote with fixed weights applied to single

models outputs, without any kind of learnable input-content based routing to the specialist

models. This static process cannot exploit potential complementary specialization of

specialist models as all inputs are processed in the same way. A highly contrast drusen

photograph should obviously be classified to the AMD specialist and a very slight optic

disc asymmetry should strongly contribute to aGlaucomalevel, something impossible with

static fusion schemes. Static ensemble methods also suffer from "routing collapse" in the

case of non-optimally trained gating networks, whereby every image is classified with

certainty towards a single (perhaps poorly trained) expert, nullifying the value of

specialization. The system described below tackles both these issues with Architecture

the GateDiversityLoss to discourage collapsing through entropy regularization.
section_heading: 1.2.4 Gap III — Static Fusion Without Learnable Routing

text:
Bio-inspired optimization algorithms have appeared in the literature on classification of

retinal disease as a pre-processing stage to assist with feature selection of handcrafted

features, and as a post-hoc mechanism to optimize hyper parameters of shallow machine

learning classifiers. No prior published work has integrated multiple bio-inspired

algorithms simultaneously within the training loop of a deep learning system for multi-

disease retinal classification — operating at the level of attention weights, loss function

parameters, decision thresholds, fusion routing, and feature mixing simultaneously. It's

absence represented a major opportunity to use bio-inspired algorithms as they are

specifically tailored to search complex, non-convex, multi-modal optimisation spaces.
section_heading: 1.2.5 Gap IV — Absence of Bio-Inspired Integration Within Deep Training Loops

text:
Over-confident models that are constantly producing incorrect predictions with high levels

of certainty are more dangerous than models that are simply producing incorrect

predictions, since clinicians are likely to regard erroneous predictions as fact without

questioning. Deep neural networks are notoriously badly calibrated on smaller or

imbalanced data sets. Yet none of the existing retinal disease classification systems

surveyed in the literature review for this thesis incorporate a differentiable Expected

Calibration Error (ECE) term as a training-time loss component. This paper is the first to

apply an ECE calibration loss at the HG-MEF-Bio architecture's fusion layer in order to
section_heading: 1.2.6 Gap V — Clinical Trust, Calibration, and Explainability

text:
The need for this research is rooted in the vast and increasing global demand for screening

of retinal diseases in the presence of an even larger deficit of trained human graders. Currently, over 537 million people worldwide suffer from diabetes, all of whom are at risk

of developing DR, and all of whom ideally should be screened with fundus examination

each year. Combining the populations at risk for AMD (ages >50; in particular those with

family history) and Glaucoma (high IOP, family history, ages >40), over 1.5 billion

individuals are at risk worldwide and need regular ophthalmic screening. The ratio of ophthalmologists per person is however below 3 per 100,000 people in LMICs

(responsible for the largest burden of disease) compared to greater than 12 per 100,000 in

HICs. It is not possible to achieve annual fundus screening of all patients with risk factors

for diabetic retinopathy (DR) with the current workforce even if all 30,000 of India's

ophthalmologists work full-time on DR screening in the leading contributor to blind from

diabetes. The development of AI algorithms that analyze fundus images to ophthalmologist

level accuracy is thus the only technically feasible method to enable population scale

screening for retinal disease given human resource constraints.
section_heading: 1.3.1 The Growing Universal Need for Retinal Screening

text:
In reality retinal screening is multi-disease. A diabetic screening patient may have an early

stage of glaucoma (which is a relatively common co-morbidity, given that diabetic

microvascular damage occurs elsewhere other than just in the retinal vasculature). An

elderly patient presenting with visual symptoms could have AMD, Glaucoma or a

combination of both. A single-disease AI running on a tele-ophthalmology pipeline only

produces the output for the single disease it was trained on, therefore each stage of a

pipeline has to go through many individual single-disease AIs, each one has its own

computational/integration cost, and possible contradictory outputs, hence a clear case for

merging them all together into one multi-disease system on both the operational and

clinical front.
section_heading: 1.3.2 The Inadequacy of Single-Disease Systems for Real-World Deployment

text:
One pass of our proposed HG-MEF architecture allows for the simultaneous

classification of images into AMD (4 categories), Glaucoma (2 referral grades) and DR (5

severity grades), providing an all-round assessment of a patients retinal health from a single

fundus image, reducing computational cost while overcoming many of the operational

costs of dealing with many single-disease AI models. There is an architectural imperative to an expert-then-fuse method rather than a simple

single, unified multi-disease model arising from the three diseases themselves. The three

diseases: AMD, Glaucoma, and DR produce evidence patterns which are not merely

visually different, but which involve different anatomical systems (macula, optic disc, and

retinal microvasculature respectively), and involve different scales and best input pre-

processing approaches suited for each individual disease.
section_heading: 1.3.2 The Inadequacy of Single-Disease Systems for Real-World Deployment

text:
The visual disparity of the three

diseases implies that an identical feature-extraction architecture across all three diseases

will inevitably suffer compromises, both for the specialized task of each, that would be

structurally circumvented by expert-then-fuse where the feature-extraction networks could

learn optimal specialized features per disease. Quantitative backing of specialization's

importance is substantial, as the Architecture 1 AMD expert trained only on AMD yields

97.75% accuracy, a metric the unified Phase-I ViT could not even come close to for AMD

alone; and similarly for glaucoma's 94.4% accuracy in the binary referral classification

task. The scope of this paper is more than just fusion network construction but also

reasoning for a disease-specific training strategy so that the "expert-then-fuse" framework
section_heading: 1.3.2 The Inadequacy of Single-Disease Systems for Real-World Deployment

text:
The clinical severity of failure on the minority class in DR classification suggests the need

for a principled algorithm, instead of just simple data augmentation strategies. The most

urgent stage of classification (for the clinician) from an immediate treatment viewpoint is

the Severe DR stage. This is defined by > 20 retinal hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants, venous

beading and conspicuous IRMA. Patients identified as Severe DR are at 50% risk of

progressing to the ultimate vision-threatening stage (Proliferative DR) within 1 year and

requires immediate physician attention. A classification system that only detects 39% of

Severe DR cases as demonstrated by Architecture 1 is medically inappropriate and

dangerous. Therefore, the requirement for the three DR specific methods developed herein

(SOL1, SOL2, SOL3) is not theoretical but an immediate patient safety requirement. There

has been no prior publication of a deep learning system for DR classification that has

employed PSO based in-training threshold penalisation, GA based recall-floor constraint

evolution and recall-aware head diversity loss for alleviating minority class failure given

the clinic-relevant class distribution of DR. SOL1+SOL2+SOL3 achieved a clinical gain

of 53.5 pp in Severe DR classification which is immediately useful in the practical clinic.
section_heading: 1.3.4 The Need for Algorithmic Solutions to Minority Class Failure

text:
Clinicians and regulators want to see beyond the AI output-they want AI systems to provide

statistically-calibrated estimates of confidence, explanations which are aligned with

clinical knowledge and imaging conventions and a validated characteristic of

robustness.1The current work contributes three mechanisms that provide this: Firstly,

inclusion of Grad-CAM explainability in the expert models and comparison of the

predicted attention with the true location of lesions, secondly, a novel inclusion of a

differentiable ECE calibration loss at the fusion level which ensures that the predicted class

probabilities correspond to the observed empirical classification certainty, and thirdly,

design of a PSO based post-training threshold optimisation method to set the operating

decision boundary to a specified clinical specification – such as maximising sensitivity at

a controlled level of specificity for highly specific conditions like Severe DR and Referable

This is one of the most rapidly developing areas of medical AI within the past ten years;

fueled by large-scale annotated datasets of fundus images, the emergence of powerful deep

learning architectures, and a vital clinical need for a system supporting scaled screening. In this literature review, we consolidate 33 research papers and pre-prints published within

the last five years (2020-2025) into 6 main clusters: 1) CNN-based automated retinal

disease classification; 2) Vision Transformers and CNN-ViT hybrids; 3) multi-disease and

multi-label retinal screening; 4) ensembles in retinal screening; 5) attention mechanisms

for retinal feature extraction; and 6) bio-inspired optimization in medical imaging. Finally,

the literature review ends with a summary table and categorical list of current research gaps

which are the direct motivation behind the innovative network architectures that can be

seen in HG-MEF and HG-MEF-Bio below.

The structuring of this literature review reflects

the timeline of this field as it developed from single-disease, single model to multi-disease,

hybrid, and ensemble solutions, and eventually to bio-inspired search methods; this

temporal progression represents more than time passing; rather, it marks a recognition of

specific obstacles in this field such as class imbalance, intra-class feature impurity, domain

The foundational era of deep learning-based retinal disease classification was dominated

by Convolutional Neural Networks, which demonstrated the feasibility of replacing hand-

crafted feature engineering with end-to-end learned representations. This category of work

establishes the performance baselines against which the more sophisticated architectures

text:
There have been historically two parallel types of frameworks to consider the task of multi-

disease retinal classification. These include: (a) flat multi-label or multi-class models that

produce all the diseases to one unified fused space [9, 14, 15, 16, 20, 33] and (b) single-

disease expert models which do not fuse to a common representation and are trained

individually [2, 3, 5, 6, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28]. Of all the system frameworks we surveyed,

there isn't any attempt to learn an expert knowledge specific to a disease AND merge them

into a single, multi-disease output using an expert-then-fuse framework based on learning-

This gap causes an intrinsic accuracy compromise. The loss in per-disease accuracy when

flat, multi-disease models are considered cannot be achieved by single-disease experts. Single-disease specialists can not function as overall screening tools. The HG-MEF

architecture attempts to bridge this gap by having three individually trained disease specific

expert models fused together via a learned hierarchical fusion network with dynamic

gating, which yields specialist-level per-disease accuracy (AMD: 97.75%, Glaucoma:

94.4%, DR: 86.8% on Architecture 1; better on Architecture 2: 97.25%, 95.45%, 93.6%)

section_heading: 2.9.2 Gap 2 — Bio-Inspired Algorithms Are Not Integrated Within Deep Learning

text:
Several works have illustrated that published DR classification systems systematically

under-perform on Severe and Proliferative DR [1, 3, 22, 23, 27], but it is not a problem that

has been simultaneously and algorithmically addressed on all three levels of loss function

formulation, decision threshold tuning, and diversity of heads. Common solutions:

oversampling, class-weighted cross-entropy and augmentation have each been individually

applied and failed. Standard remedies alone never worked for an acceptable sensitivity for

the clinically essential minority classes when run with class imbalance. The dual problem of Wet AMD sensitivity (96.56% accuracy overall but 89.45%

sensitivity) was addressed by Abdullahi et al. [5] who advocated for cost sensitive learning

and SMOTE type solutions. Architecture 1 confirms that the most advanced class-weighted

cross-entropy solutions combined with augmentation cannot sufficiently resolve Severe

DR (39.3% recall). Architecture 2, with three novel solutions designed specifically for

DR,SOL1,SOL2, andSOL3, represents the first known simultaneous multi-mechanism

approach to the problem and represents a 53.5% gain over standard methods on Severe DR.

text:
The comparative analysis table (Table 2.1) provides a structured mapping of

each work's methodological characteristics, enabling direct identification of five research

gaps: the absence of disease-specific expert-then-fuse architectures with dynamic gating;

the non-integration of bio-inspired algorithms within deep training loops; the unresolved

minority class failure in DR grading; the absence of ECE calibration loss in retinal

classification training; and the absence of entropy-regularised learnable gating in retinal

These five gaps collectively define the research contributions of the proposed HG-MEF

and HG-MEF-Bio systems, as detailed in Chapter 3. Each gap is addressed by a specific

DiseaseSpecificGatingNetwork (Gap 1), the six integrated bio-inspired algorithms (Gap

2), the SOL1/SOL2/SOL3 DR-specific solutions (Gap 3), the ECE calibration loss (Gap

4), and the GateDiversityLoss (Gap 5) — ensuring that the proposed system constitutes a

principled and complete response to the identified deficiencies in the existing literature.

In this paper, a hierarchy multi-expert fusion system is proposed for automated and

simultaneous detection of three main retinal diseases (AMD, Glaucoma, and DR) in

color fundus image. The top level framework is the expert-then-fuse paradigm, in which

three expert deep learning models were individually trained for each disease using the

individual data set and the trained models are fused into an ensemble learned fusion

network to output a single multi-disease classification. The framework deliberately

avoids the inter-class feature collision as in naive combined single model architecture. In the naive single model approach, multiple disease supervision signals compete for

the gradients from back-propagation, and therefore "hurts" the expertise of the

The system is delivered as two complete architectures.

Architecture 1 — the

Hierarchical Gating Multi-Expert Fusion (HG-MEF) — employs standard deep

learning components without bio-inspired optimisation, establishing a rigorous non-bio

baseline. In this Architecture 2 (Bio-Inspired HG-MEF-Bio) each non-differentiable

architectural choice present in Architecture 1 was substituted and supported by one or

more bio-inspired metaheuristics algorithms working at: attention weight optimization,

loss function parameters evolution, decision threshold tuning, fusion routing fine-

tuning, and feature contribution weights. By using these two architectures we could

show controlled ablation of the bio-inspired mechanisms and a quantifiable

Architecture 1 consists of four trained models: EnhancedAMDModel (4 classes),

HybridGlaucomaModel (2 classes), HybridDRModel (5 classes), and the

HierarchicalMultiExpertFusion network (12 unified classes). The three expert models

are trained independently on their respective datasets.

Upon completion, their backbone

weights are frozen and the HG-MEF fusion network is trained on top of their outputs. The unified taxonomy comprises twelve classes: Normal, AMD, Cataract, NRG, RG,

Architecture 2 is similar to Architecture 1 but with bio-augmented experts

instead of three expert models, and HierarchicalBioExpertFusion (HG-MEF-Bio) is

used instead of the fusion network. It produces eleven merged classes (the 'Multiple'

class is excluded from the mutually exclusive taxonomy). In this architecture, six bio-

inspired algorithms (FA, GWO, GA, PSO, ABC and DE) were incorporated throughout

the training process, at all levels of the architecture. A three separate DR solutions were

incorporated, the DR1, DR2, and DR3, in order to address the most crucial issue of

failure in the minority class in Architecture 1.

corresponding to one disease domain. All datasets contain two-dimensional colour

DE runs every 6 epochs during fusion training over 20 generations. SOL1 is the first of three dedicated solutions to the DR minority class problem. In

standard practice, PSO is applied post-training as a threshold calibration step. SOL1

extends this by incorporating PSO-optimised thresholds directly into the training loss

during the DR expert model training, creating a co-evolutionary feedback loop between

Every 10 training epochs, a PSO run is executed on a small validation subset to find the

current best per-class decision thresholds θ_PSO ∈ ℝ^5 for the five DR classes. These

thresholds are then used to define an additional training loss that penalises the model

whenever its predicted probability for the correct class falls below the corresponding

L_SOL1 = λ_SOL1 · mean_i( ReLU( θ_PSO[y_i] − p_{y_i} ) )

where y_i is the true class label for sample i, p_{y_i} is the predicted softmax

probability for that class, and θ_PSO[y_i] is the PSO-optimised threshold for class

y_i.

The ReLU operator only allows the loss to fire when the model is not confident

about its prediction (under threshold); if it is overconfident on a correct prediction there

is no penalty. We introduced a loss co-efficient SO L1 = 0.2 to trade off this penalty

with the normal classfication losses. This mechanism whereby PSO determines

thresholds for the current weakness of the model, and these thresholds cause the model

to become more confident on the minority class(es), are the reason for the Huge increase

of Severe DR accuracy from 39.3% to 92.8%

SOL2 modifies the Genetic Algorithm fitness function used for class weight

evolutionto incorporate a hard recall floor constraint and a hard-class recall bonus. In

Architecture 1, fixed class weights [1.0, 2.0, 1.5, 3.0, 3.5] for the five DR classes are

insufficient to prevent the model from sacrificing minority class recall in favour of

overall accuracy — a consequence of the 10:1 imbalance between No_DR  and

Severe SOL2 replaces the standard macro-F1 GA fitness with a clinically informed

Fitness(ω) = MacroF1(ω) − 2.0 · Σ_k max(0, 0.55 − recall_k(ω)) + 0.1 · Σ_{j ∈ H}

Where 5 is the class weight vector being evolved, recallk() is the per class recall on the

validation set obtained using these weights and H = {Mild, Proliferative, Severe} is the

set of hard minority classes.

The first term is the objective, the second is a lower bound

on recall, at which any class whose recall is below 0.55, loses 2 points for every

percentage point that its recall is below 0.55, making it the strongest penalty and thus

dominating (20 greater than the hard class bonus), while the third term acts as a reward

for further increasing recall on the three hardest classes. As an extra condition, the

NoDR weight has been clamped at 1.5. This stops the GA from collapsing the dominant

NoDR weight to 0, a degenerate solution, while still maximizing minority class fitness,

thus satisfying the clinical condition that NoDR class must always be classified

correctly The GA class weights evolved by SOL2 reached values of up to 4.9 for the

Severe class across different GA runs, compared to the fixed weight of 3.5 in

SOL3 replaces the symmetric PenalisedAgreementLoss with a recall-aware asymmetric

L_SOL3 = −0.2 · Σ_{c ∈ H} KL(p_c^(1) || p_c^(2)) + 0.1 · Σ_{c ∈ E}

where H = {Mild, Proliferative, Severe} (hard classes — encourage head divergence to

prevent both heads from confidently misclassifying), E = {No_DR, Moderate} (easy

classes — penalise divergence to maintain consistency on well-understood grades).

All experiments from both phase-I and phase-II were performed on GPU-accelerated

computing hardware. The Phase-I training was performed using Google Colab Pro (on an

NVIDIA Tesla T4 16GB VRAM) and the GPU offered enough throughput to execute both

single-model CNN and Vision Transformer training pipelines. Phase-II training was

performed on a local machine with an NVIDIA RTX A4000 16GB VRAM allowing to run

the 3-backbone Architecture 2 experts without losing any state with a complete checkpoint

persistence strategy and with the required bfloat16 Automatic Mixed Precision. The software stack used was based on python 3.12 and Pytorch 2.0+ as the core deep

learning framework. The other major libraries include: torchvision for general image

timm(PyTorch Image Models) to obtain pre-trained ViT-B/16 and EfficientNet-B4

backbone for initialization, scikit-learn for AUC-ROC and classification report calculation,

and Matplotlib and Seaborn for visualizing the training curve and convergence.

All the

model checkpoint files for Phase-II used an atomic write-verify-replace (writing to .pth.tmp

and then only if correct loading was successful writing to .pth by rename) mechanism to

reduce likelihood of checkpoint corruption on long training sessions. Custom function for

cleaning the state-dictionary keys were implemented to remove origmod. Prefix coming

from calling torch.compile() in Colab when models of Phase-I were moved to VS code

All three of the repositories available for public access were used over the two project

stages. Both of the EyePACS and APTOS 2019 datasets were used for Diabetic

Retinopathy (DR), which contains fundus images for five classification categories; no

DR, mild NPDR, moderate NPDR, severe NPDR and proliferative DR. Both the

AMDNet and HYAMD repositories were used for Age-Related Macular Degeneration

(AMD), which has four classification categories; AMD, Cataract, Diabetes and Normal.

Both of the REFUGE and ORIGA benchmark datasets were used for Glaucoma which

was classified into two binary labels; Non-Referable Glaucoma (NRG) and Referable

In phase I, all three disease datasets were clubbed together into one directory, diseases

having their names prepended to filenames and divided 60/20/20 into

training/validation/test set keeping stratified class distributions of the datasets. In phase

II, datasets are kept individual to diseases and class distributions are 70/15/15 stratified

split. The validation sets had 400 samples for AMD (100 samples for each class), 770 for

Glaucoma (385 for each class) and 607 for the test set of DR (No_DR: 169, Mild: 108,

Moderate: 155, Proliferative: 106, Severe: 69). A radius validity check was performed in

the pre-processing to reject noisy images.

Any fundus image where the detected radius

for retinal structure is less than 50 pixels was rejected for all splits. A single preprocessing pipeline was utilized for all diseases in Phase-I. These included

automated circular retinal region cropping based on intensity thresholding, Ben-Graham

weighted subtraction using a Gaussian filter (sigma=10) for enhancing the vessels and

edges, extraction of green channel which contains the largest range of lesion pixels,

CLAHE for equalizing the local contrast and image size normalization to 224x224 and

There were three motivated medical preprocessing steps applied in Phase-II (one per

disease). For AMD and DR, the entire Ben-Graham pipeline was used with output

resolution 512 512. For Glaucoma, a new pipeline was built: retina masking using an

intensity threshold and largest contour detection followed by CLAHE on the green

channel only (clipLimit = 2.0, tileGridSize = 8) 8, skipping the illumination correction

step not to alter the cup-to-disk morphology which is the dominant symptom in glaucoma

classification.

The augmentation policies were also specific for each disease: 2 (uniform)

for AMD, class-aware for DR using 3 for mild DR, 4 for severe and proliferative DR and

limited augmentation (horizontal flip, 5 rotation, 0.1 brightness) for Glaucoma as optic

For all the models, phases, and architectures the following evaluation metrics were used:

• Overall Accuracy: the accuracy of all class labels; it is the main summed up

• Per-Class accuracy: it is the accuracy of each of the classes (diagonal of the

confusion matrix), thus the performance of each minority class is taken into account

(e.g. Serious DR); it also represents the main figure for the evaluation of a specific

• Macro-averaged F1 Score: a per-class F1 Score averaged over all classes so that

each class has a weight.

This is the target for optimizing the DR models since we

• Weighted F1 score: an F1 Score averaged over each class with weight of samples

per class; this is an evaluation figure for imbalanced classes when a reduction in

class imbalance is not desired (thus can be used in a fusion model, because different

classes could likely have different number of training data).

• AUC-ROC (One-vs-Rest): area under the ROC curve, it evaluates class separation

• Confusion Matrix: it is a specialized version for the purpose that it allows us to

identify systematically different kinds of errors between classes of different degree

• Bio-Algorithm Fitness: the results shown are the performance for each bio-inspired

algorithm for iterations; the FA fitness curve was monitored for a single run; the

best fitness achieved by the GWO population; the macro-F1 for GA for each run;

For Phase-I training, five CNN architectures (VGG16, ResNet-50, DenseNet-121,

InceptionV3 and MobileNetV2) were trained using ImageNet-pretrained weights and a 10-

layer Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16). All the models were trained on the combined four-

class dataset (AMD, DR, Glaucoma, Healthy) in a 60-20-20 train/validation/test split. The

CNN models were trained with the Adam optimiser with the learning rate initially set to

25-40 epochs (depending on model performance and validation loss). The Vision

Transformer was trained up to 120 epochs with cosine decay and a warm-up schedule, a

regularization method in the form of swarm-inspired attention sparsification, and with

Phase-II Architecture 1 used an expert-then-fuse approach, where 3 disease specific expert

models were trained independently prior to training the fusion network. The AMD Expert

(EnhancedAMDModel) was trained using Adam (LR = 0.0001) and ReduceLROnPlateau

(HybridDRModel) was trained using CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts and class weighted

cross-entropy (higher penalties for Severe, Mild, and Proliferative stages) for 17 epochs.

lacks the ability to adjust decision boundaries with such an imbalance scenario. So this

In this thesis we design, implement and evaluate the Bio-Inspired Hierarchical Gating

Multi-Expert Fusion (HG-MEF-Bio) system to automate the classification of the 3 most

prevalent retinal diseases - Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD), Glaucoma and

Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) based on colour fundus photograph. The thesis was organized

into two project stages and two entire architectures where innovations are progressively

made at both stages, providing concrete and clinically useful gains. This work's main architectural contribution is the expert-then-fuse approach. As the system

consists of three separately trained, disease-specific expert networks that are then fused

together using a learned hierarchical fusion network, the proposed method avoids inter-

class feature interference, which degrades naive, multi-disease, expert fusion. The

Architecture 1 HG-MEF baseline demonstrated that this paradigm yields specialist-level

accuracy across all three disease domains simultaneously: AMD at 97.75%, Glaucoma at

94.4%, and DR at 86.8% — substantially exceeding the Phase-I unified Vision

Transformer's performance on a significantly more demanding eleven-class taxonomy.

The six bio-inspired optimisation algorithms — Firefly Algorithm (FA), Grey Wolf

Optimiser (GWO), Genetic Algorithm (GA), Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO),

Artificial Bee Colony (ABC), and Differential Evolution (DE) — were integrated as active

training-loop participants across every level of the Architecture 2 HG-MEF-Bio system. The most clinically significant result of the entire research programme is the 53.5

percentage point improvement in Severe DR classification accuracy, rising from 39.3% in

Architecture 1 to 92.8% in Architecture 2 through the combined action of SOL1 (PSO in-

training threshold penalty), SOL2 (GA recall-floor constraint evolution), and SOL3

(Recall-Aware Diversity Loss). This is of direct patient safety relevance: a screening

mechanism correctly classifying 92.8% of Severe DR against the 39.3% accuracy of

Architecture 1 avoided many more cases of omitted referrals of patients for immediate

laser/anti-VEGF treatment which would otherwise result in irreversible loss of sight.

The end-to-end HG-MEF-Bio fusion model obtained a validation accuracy of 95.14% and

macro-F1 of 0.9278 at Epoch 10 of 50 of its training course - and at this stage already

bettered Architecture 1's 90.63% accuracy and 0.9057 F1 achieved after 30 full epochs. The ABC-corrected routing network solved the AMD Expert under-utilization problem

identified in Architecture 1 and the DEFeatureMixer gave an instant +1.2 percentage point

accuracy improvement after it was applied for the first time at Epoch 6. The integration of

a differentiable Expected Calibration Error (ECE) loss at the fusion level represents the

first published application of training-time calibration regularisation in multi-disease

retinal classification, ensuring that the system's reported confidence levels are statistically

reliable for clinical decision support.

These outcomes taken together support the main

hypothesis that, when directly built into, rather than attached as tuners to the training-loop,

bio-inspired algorithms can overcome precisely the failure cases which pure gradient-based

learning with fixed weights and fixed augmentations fails to solve (minority class

imbalance, route collapse and incorrectly calibrated decisions). To summarize, we've

shown a monotonic, architecture driven path from ~90% unifying accuracy over 4 broad

disease categories (Phase-I ViT) to 95.14% intermediate accuracy over 11 detailed clinical

gradations (Architecture 2 HG-MEF-Bio), and developed a justified, interpretable and

clinically extensible approach to population scale, AI driven retinal disease screening. Despite the advantages of the system, some important directions of future research are

evident from both the success and failures obtained from this work.

They are as follows. All results reported in this thesis are based on well-known publicly available benchmark

datasets. For future development, more effort needs to be spent on future validation with

future clinical fundus image, different imaging modalities(i.e. Zeiss Visucam, Topcon

TRC, Remidio non-mydriatic camera), different cohort of patients, different site (e.g. LMICs with highest DR & glaucoma prevalence), there might be benefit in cross-modality

generalization with adversarial feature alignment or test time augmentation

The current system only relies on the 2D colour fundus photograph. Supplementing the

information source, e.g. Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) which produces thickness

measurement for individual retinal layers across a cross-section, can be highly beneficial

to the features available for the expert systems, specifically for subtle changes occurring in

early stage AMD and glaucoma. A possible further work is a dual stream expert system

that inputfundus and OCT image for each disease area and fusing by existing cross

attention module, which have a good clinical logic. The present 3-backbone expert architecture needs about 16 GB VRAM for training and a

large number of computational resources to perform inference. The next research work is

to study the possibilities to transfer knowledge between the full HG-MEF-Bio teacher and

a small student model by training on student model by mimic the logits and attention maps

from the teacher model for deployment. For edge device and tele-ophthalmology system

Objectives The aim of the study is to emphasize and explore the possible transtemporal approaches for spectrum of complicated lateral skull base pathologies. Design Retrospective analysis of complicated lateral skull base pathologies was managed in our institute between January 2017 and December 2019. Setting The study was conducted in a tertiary care referral center. Main Outcome Measures The study focused on the selection of approach based on site and extent of the pathology, the surgical nuances for each approach, and the associated complications. Results A total of 10 different pathologies of the lateral skull base were managed by different transtemporal approaches. The most common complication encountered was facial nerve palsy (43%, n ¼ 6). Other complications included cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) collection (15%, n ¼ 2), cosmetic deformity (24%, n ¼ 4), petrous internal carotid artery injury (7%, n ¼ 1), and hypoglossal nerve palsy (7%, n ¼ 1). The cosmetic deformity included flap necrosis (n ¼ 2) and postoperative bony defects leading to contour defects of the scalp (n ¼ 2). Conclusion Surgical approach should be tailored based on the individual basis, to obtain adequate exposure and complete excision. Selection of appropriate surgical approach should also be based on the training and preference of the operating surgeon. Whenever necessary, combined surgical approaches facilitating full tumor exposure are recommended so that complete tumor excision is feasible. This requires a multidisciplinary team comprising neurosurgeons, neuro-otologist, neuroanesthetist, and plastic surgeons. The surgeon must know precise microsurgical anatomy to preserve the adjacent nerves and vessels, which is necessary for better surgical outcomes.

text: The anatomy of the temporal bone, its complex, intimate, and intricate anatomical relationship to the skull base structures makes the management of the lesions in the vicinity very challenging. The temporal bone has five parts: squamosal, petrous, mastoid, tympanic, and styloid process. Temporal bone pathologies usually present with symptoms of hearing deficit (conductive, sensorineural, mixed), vestibular dysfunction, facial nerve dysfunction, mastication difficulties, and dysphagia. Imaging plays an essential role in the determination of the exact location of the lesion along with the relationship of the lesion with surrounding neurovascular structures and may suggest the differential diagnosis of pathologies. Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are often complementary to each other, and in most cases, both are required.

A surgical approach is defined as the route taken for the surgical procedure from an opening to the target. Various approaches are currently available for the management of temporal bone pathologies. 1, 2 Usually, two or more approaches are combined for the same lesion; therefore, intimate knowledge of anatomy and multidisciplinary evaluation are essential factors to be considered in choosing an appropriate approach for this complex area. This ensures both effective treatment of pathology and better functional and cosmetic outcomes. The knowledge of the structures we encounter in any particular approach is vital along with the judgment of which are to be preserved, mobilized, or removed.

text: It determines the success of choosing the particular surgical corridor for particular lesion and accessibility. The selection of the approach used depends upon the type of pathology whether benign or malignant, site of origin, and extension which may be confined to temporal bone or extending to the adjacent areas of the neck, infratemporal fossa, and in the "exo" and "endo" cranial regions or both. Rhoton Jr 2 classified the temporal approaches into three categories. It is essential to consider multiple factors during the surgical planning to get a good functional outcome, which is cosmetically appealing with minimal morbidity at the end. It includes proper skin flap design without compromising its vascularity, especially while doing the revision cases. Proper dissection and preservation of muscle and musculoperiosteal flap are also important to ensure a tight cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) closure as well as obliteration of the surgical cavity at the end of surgery. The approach should give adequate exposure and straight-line access to the pathology with minimal to no brain retraction and be versatile enough to expand intraoperatively. The need for preoperative embolization and intraoperative measures to tackle blood loss is planned well before the intervention. The present review enumerates the challenging case scenarios that we have managed through the transtemporal approaches.

text: Extended cortical mastoidectomy involves complete exenteration of mastoid air cells with skeletonization of surrounding anatomical structures, while a conventional cortical mastoidectomy involves removal of the mastoid cortex and opening of the mastoid antrum. Extended mastoidectomy is performed using microsurgical cutting and diamond burr with continuous suction and irrigation. The initial step was by using postauricular incision; skin flaps and musculoperiosteal flap were raised; outer mastoid cortex air cells were drilled out followed by opening of the mastoid antrum and identification of the lateral semicircular canal, which is the most reliable landmark in the temporal bone and helps in the identification of facial nerve and bony labyrinth. Bone is removed from the sinodural angle and along the superior petrosal sinus. The mastoid air cells are exenterated from the sinodural angle, tegmen, and posterior fossa dural plate areas.

text: A 55-year-old gentleman is a known case of left vestibular schwannoma, he underwent left Retro-mastoid-sub-occipital (RMSO) craniectomy and excision of the tumor 11 years ago. During that surgery the left eighth cranial nerve was sacrificed, while the left seventh cranial nerve was preserved. Now, he presented with left hemi-facial spasm and left-sided gait ataxia, on MRI there was an evidence of recurrence of the lesion for which he underwent re-exploration of left RMSO craniectomy and gross total excision recurrence was done. Two months after the second surgery, he came with complaints of watery discharge from the nose. CT cisternography showed a CSF tract from the operated cavity filling the mastoid cavity through the supra labyrinthine tract into the middle ear and through the Eustachian tube into the nasal cavity. The patient was planned for extended cortical mastoidectomy and repair of the fistulous tract. The left postauricular incision was made followed by extended cortical mastoidectomy. Tegmen, posterior fossa dural plate, labyrinthine block, and sigmoid sinus were delineated and preserved. CSF leak through the supralabyrinthine cell tract was identified (►Fig. 1A and B) and demarked to be reconstructed with musculoperiosteal tissue and fat. Aditus was blocked with fat. Fibrin glue was applied (►Fig. 1C).

text: Extended cortical mastoidectomy is the preferred approach in cases where hearing preservation is required. However, there are many situations where hearing is already lost, and the pathology involves the middle ear cleft where a more radical approach is needed in the form of radical mastoidectomy. The difference between a radical mastoidectomy and extended cortical mastoidectomy is that the posterior canal wall was taken down along with the removal of middle ear structures like ossicles (except stapes footplate) along with the obliteration of Eustachian tube opening into the middle ear. The facial nerve within the fallopian canal was delineated and preserved.

text: However, there are certain indications in which surgical excision should be preferred. The reason for choosing surgery over RT in two patients included in this series is the involvement of 12th cranial nerve in one patient and young age (32 years) in the second case. The patient was planned for surgical excision via a transtemporal route. The craniotemporocervical incision was made; control of the major vessels was obtained in the neck followed by extended canal wall mastoidectomy. Vertical and tympanic segments of the facial nerve were mobilized; a tumor in the middle ear and external auditory canal was gradually debulked with bipolar electrocautery. The tympanic bone was drilled, and jugular foramen was exposed. Sigmoid sinus was extraluminally packed and obliterated following, which IJV was ligated and cut. Lateral wall of IJV along with the tumor in the IJV (►Fig. 4B), jugular bulb, and hypotympanum were removed with the preservation of medial wall of IJV (►Fig. 4C). Brisk bleed from the inferior petrous sinus was controlled with Surgicel and gel foam. The tumor cavity was obliterated with fat, and blind-sac closure of the EAC was performed. Another case of a hypoglossal schwannoma presenting as jugular foramen lesion was also managed with this approach successfully with some modifications (►Fig. 4D and E ).

text: Radical mastoidectomy is chosen in cases where the petrous apex/bony labyrinth is spared. However, in cases with the disease involving the middle ear cleft but extending into the labyrinth or a primary disease of the petrous bone with hearing loss, a transcochlear approach can be used. The transcochlear approach is mainly useful for lesion involving the petrous apex and adjoining areas with hearing loss. House and Hitselberger have initially described the transcochlear approach; it includes identification of the internal auditory canal, posterior rerouting of the facial nerve, and removal of the cochlea and petrous apex with the preservation of middle ear and EAC 3 . In modified transcochlear approach, we combine the removal of the middle ear and external auditory canal with posterior re-routing of the facial nerve; this widens the exposure and allows better control of the temporal carotid artery and ease the complete removal of petrous apex lesion. 4 We had two rare cases involving the temporal bone, (1) Petrous apex recurrent chondrosarcoma and (2) Fibrous dysplasia of temporal bone which were managed by the modified transcochlear approach.

text: A 45-year-old female presented with complaints of neck mass with headache, who had undergone surgery 4 years back and was a histologically proven case of petrous chondrosarcoma. MRI brain showed a large peripherally enhancing lobulated lesion in cerebellopontine angle (►Fig. 2A and B) extending from lower pons to C2 level, at the site of jugular foramen with the cystic component in cerebellar hemisphere associated with cerebellar edema. The pathology replaced the temporal bone (petrous and mastoid part). There was also a well-defined lesion in the left side of the mid-neck. A left craniotemporocervical incision was made. Through a modified transcochlear approach, the tumor debulking was performed, and complete excision was done (►Fig. 2C and D). Through the same incision, the tumor in the neck was excised. The dural repair was done with the artificial dura and tumor cavity was obliterated with fat. Skin closure was done in multiple layers.

text: A 21-yearold male presented with right-sided painless swelling behind the ear with ear discharge for 4 years. He had undergone two surgeries for the same complaints in the past 8 years. After the second surgery he developed facial nerve palsy. The histopathology showed fibrous dysplasia. CT showed a well-defined lytic lesion replacing the entire temporal bone, with the displacement of the cerebellum. MRI showed well-defined large nonenhancing lesion involving the right temporal bone with significant compression on the intracranial structures (►Fig. 2E). Due to multiple recurrences, we planned for a radical excision. A right craniotemporocervical incision was made (►Fig. 2F), and the tumor was gradually debulked and separated from the middle fossa dura. As the tumor was densely adherent to the posterior fossa dura, during resection, there was rent in the dura, which was repaired using artificial dura. Due to multiple surgeries, there was skin flap necrosis, which was managed nonsurgically. Cranioplasty was planned at a later stage.

text: Transcochlear approach is preferred for lesions of the petrous apex with hearing loss and is a more radical approach. However, for lesions of the petrous apex with preserved hearing, one can use the middle fossa approach which is a more conservative approach. A classical middle fossa approach provides a subtemporal extradural approach to the middle fossa floor and is most commonly used for the excision of vestibular schwannoma situated laterally in the internal auditory canal. 5, 6 The extended middle fossa approach provides exposure to the lesion that extends to the petrous apex and supraclival region.

text: A 51-year-old male, with a known case of right middle ear adenoma who had undergone surgery 3 years ago, presented with a headache. MRI showed a sharp contrast-enhancing lesion in the right petrous temporal bone (►Fig. 3A), right half of clivus and right occipital condyle encasing right ICA with the involvement of IAM with the encasement of intracanalicular part of right seven to eight cranial nerve complex extending into the ipsilateral cerebellopontine angle and mastoid air cells which were suggestive of recurrence. The CECT head showed the right frontotemporal craniotomy cavity with residual lesion along the lateral and posterior margins of the surgical cavity. The patient underwent near-total excision by extended middle fossa approach (►Fig. 3B). During the procedure, the patient had petrous carotid artery injury, which was managed with muscle plug and pressure. Postoperative CT angiography was done to rule out rebleed and aneurysm, which was normal. Postoperatively patient was subjected to radiotherapy (RT). The patient is under follow-up for the past 1.5 years and has no increase in the size of the lesion.

paper_journal: Journal of Neurological Surgery Part B: Skull Base
paper_abstract: Objectives The aim of the study is to emphasize and explore the possible transtemporal approaches for spectrum of complicated lateral skull base pathologies. Design Retrospective analysis of complicated lateral skull base pathologies was managed in our institute between January 2017 and December 2019. Setting The study was conducted in a tertiary care referral center. Main Outcome Measures The study focused on the selection of approach based on site and extent of the pathology, the surgical nuances for each approach, and the associated complications. Results A total of 10 different pathologies of the lateral skull base were managed by different transtemporal approaches. The most common complication encountered was facial nerve palsy (43%, n ¼ 6). Other complications included cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) collection (15%, n ¼ 2), cosmetic deformity (24%, n ¼ 4), petrous internal carotid artery injury (7%, n ¼ 1), and hypoglossal nerve palsy (7%, n ¼ 1). The cosmetic deformity included flap necrosis (n ¼ 2) and postoperative bony defects leading to contour defects of the scalp (n ¼ 2). Conclusion Surgical approach should be tailored based on the individual basis, to obtain adequate exposure and complete excision. Selection of appropriate surgical approach should also be based on the training and preference of the operating surgeon. Whenever necessary, combined surgical approaches facilitating full tumor exposure are recommended so that complete tumor excision is feasible. This requires a multidisciplinary team comprising neurosurgeons, neuro-otologist, neuroanesthetist, and plastic surgeons. The surgeon must know precise microsurgical anatomy to preserve the adjacent nerves and vessels, which is necessary for better surgical outcomes.

text: The above discussed approaches are used for lesions primarily affecting the temporal bone region including the petrous apex. However, for lesions extending from the temporal bone to the infra-temporal fossa (ITF) or lesions primarily in ITF, we need more extensive approaches. ITF is a potential space bounded by greater wing of sphenoid superiorly, and part of the temporal bone; medially by superior constrictor muscle and pterygoid plates; posteriorly by the glenoid fossa, styloid process, and carotid sheath; laterally by zygoma, mandible, parotid, and masseter muscle. Transtemporal approaches was described by Ugo Fisch (A, B, C), while the preauricular approach was described by Sekar et al. 7, 8 Fisch approaches are primarily used for lesions involving middle ear cleft with extension into jugular bulb, petrous apex, clivus, and nasopharynx. The preauricular approach gives adequate access to the petrous apex, clivus superior and inferior infratemporal fossa and nasopharynx with no middle ear or mastoid involvement.

CSF rhinorrhea is a rare complication after surgery for vestibular schwannoma. It may occur through opening up of mastoid air cells while drilling the internal auditory canal (IAC) or via the vestibule or oval window. 9 The significant factors that increase the risk of CSF rhinorrhea following vestibular schwannoma surgery are large tumor size, type of approach (retrosigmoid > translabyrinthine), and hyper pneumatized mastoid. 10, 11 CT cisternogram of temporal bone plays an essential role in diagnosing this entity and also in determining the path of CSF drainage preoperatively. 10 Treatment modalities include conservative management, lumbar drainage, or mastoid exploration with obliteration of cell tract and Eustachian tube obliteration.

The most common presentation of these lesions is a diminution of hearing and cranial nerve palsies. Surgical resection is the treatment of choice; however, piecemeal surgical resection has been associated with increased chances of local recurrence. 16 RT has a role in high-grade tumors. 17 Because of recurrence, our case underwent radical excision through extended transcochlear approach followed by RT. The preauricular transzygomatic transmandibular infratemporal approach is useful for lesion arising in the ITF and intracranial tumor arising in relation to the greater wing of the sphenoid. 21 In the case of jugular foramen exposure, removal of the styloid process along with anterior transposition of facial nerve facilitates a good exposure of jugular foramen. text: The most common tumors to occur in the region of jugular foramen are paragangliomas, schwannomas, and meningiomas. Some of the rare tumors include chondroma and chondrosarcoma. These lesions most commonly present with loss of hearing, multiple lower cranial nerve palsies, vestibular symptoms, and tinnitus. The jugular foramen lesions can be reached through a lateral corridor via transtemporal approaches, posterior approach via translabyrinthine or transcochlear route, or anterior approaches like Fisch infratemporal approach. 22 Selection of appropriate approach depends on the nature of pathology and its extension. In our series, we have managed two jugular paragangliomas and one hypoglossal nerve schwannoma through Fisch Type-A infratemporal approach. Transtemporal approaches pose particular problems to the surgeons because they have to negotiate ICA, sigmoid sinus, lower cranial nerves, seventh and eighth nerve complex, and inner ear for hearing and balance to be preserved.

text: A skull base tumor often extends into different anatomical compartments that necessitate combined approach. 22 Due to the overlap of neurosurgery and otology in this area, often collaboration between neurosurgeon and otologist is mandatory. Key to success in transtemporal approach is adequate exposure, careful attention to tissue plane while elevating the skin flap to prevent inadvertent injury to the frontal branch of the facial nerve, and to maintain the flap vascularity to prevent flap necrosis. It is also important to plan musculoperiosteal flap and muscular flaps for the reconstruction at the end of surgery. During major vessel handling, it is crucial to catch the subadventitial plane and neck control is mandatory to prevent vascular complications. The facial nerve is the most common cranial nerve at risk during transtemporal surgery.

text: Monitoring facial nerve function during the surgical procedure is mandatory whenever the facial nerve is being handled. Even with careful dissections, some degree of temporary facial nerve palsy is common due to the disturbance of its vasculature. 22 Postoperative surveillance of the nerve functioning is quite essential, especially in cases of lagophthalmos to prevent exposure keratitis. Eye moisturization using lubrication and taping of the eyelids should be initiated as early as possible. Permanent tarsorrhaphy or gold weight implantation may also be considered to avoid chronic exposure keratitis. In cases of lower cranial nerve palsies, to improve the swallowing and speech rehabilitation, a unilateral cricothyroid approximation can be done on the paralyzed side. In some studies, the cricothyroid approximation has proven to aid patients in swallowing abilities and improve their speech qualities. 23 Due to the proximity of dural space around the temporal bone, the patients undergoing transtemporal approaches are at a greater risk of developing immediate or delayed onset CSF leak. It is important to recognize the CSF leak early and decide the need for conservative management, lumbar drainage, or re-exploration as early as possible. The cosmetic deformity may arise even with careful surgical planning and reconstruction. The surgical cavity should be reconstructed with a free graft or implant at the time of surgery or a later date. 21

paper_abstract: Objectives The aim of the study is to emphasize and explore the possible transtemporal approaches for spectrum of complicated lateral skull base pathologies. Design Retrospective analysis of complicated lateral skull base pathologies was managed in our institute between January 2017 and December 2019. Setting The study was conducted in a tertiary care referral center. Main Outcome Measures The study focused on the selection of approach based on site and extent of the pathology, the surgical nuances for each approach, and the associated complications. Results A total of 10 different pathologies of the lateral skull base were managed by different transtemporal approaches. The most common complication encountered was facial nerve palsy (43%, n ¼ 6). Other complications included cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) collection (15%, n ¼ 2), cosmetic deformity (24%, n ¼ 4), petrous internal carotid artery injury (7%, n ¼ 1), and hypoglossal nerve palsy (7%, n ¼ 1). The cosmetic deformity included flap necrosis (n ¼ 2) and postoperative bony defects leading to contour defects of the scalp (n ¼ 2). Conclusion Surgical approach should be tailored based on the individual basis, to obtain adequate exposure and complete excision. Selection of appropriate surgical approach should also be based on the training and preference of the operating surgeon. Whenever necessary, combined surgical approaches facilitating full tumor exposure are recommended so that complete tumor excision is feasible. This requires a multidisciplinary team comprising neurosurgeons, neuro-otologist, neuroanesthetist, and plastic surgeons. The surgeon must know precise microsurgical anatomy to preserve the adjacent nerves and vessels, which is necessary for better surgical outcomes.

text: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a retinal disease in elderly people which deteriorate the central part of the retina. It is one of the leading causes of vision loss in the ageing persons. Every day, massive retinal images of patients with AMD are generated using the Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) and other retinal imaging modalities. It is critical that these images are automatically analysed, so as to reduce the time consumption and over reliance on clinical professionals. The advance stage of AMD which usually causes loss of sight occurs in either dry or wet form. Most of the models developed in previous studies focuses on the classification of AMD infected and normal retinal images. However, in the later stages of AMD it is necessary to determine whether the AMD is dry or wet. Ability to classify between dry and wet Age-Related Macular Degeneration is very crucial to ophthalmologists in therapeutic indication. It determines whether a patient receives Anti-VEGF injection therapy treatment. The objective of this study is to develop a convolutional neural network model that will classify between dry and wet AMD. A pretrained Deep Residual Neural Network with 50-layers (ResNet50) was used to train the model using the KERMANY dataset consisting of 32,931 OCT images of dry and wet AMD. The model was evaluated and it performed with an accuracy of 96.56%, 98.20% Specificity and 89.45% sensitivity respectively.

text: The macula which central part of the retina, is the component of the retina that is affected by AMD. It is the retina's functional core, measuring around 5mm in diameter, and when it is damaged and not handled, vision loss occurs [2] . During the course of the disease, lipid appears to collect in particles under the retinal pigment epithelium. These particles, which appear as light yellow spots on the retina, are known as drusen [3] . AMD is classified into four stages, which are normal, early AMD, Intermediate AMD, and advanced AMD. The normal or No AMD class has no or little small drusen. The Early AMD has many small drusen, handful intermediate drusen, or retinal pigment epithelium defects, Intermediate AMD class exhibit the presence of substantial intermediate drusen, at least one large drusen.

text: It is necessary to devise the ability to analyze the images from the escalating number of patients [8] . In the screening of AMD, several imaging modalities are used today [4] . The two main modalities used in the automatic detection of AMD are the optical coherence tomography (OCT) and fundus photography. Fundus photography is a non-invasive imaging procedure that involves the procedure of capturing a 2-D image of the 3-D fundus of the eye on an imaging plane, by projecting a reflected light on the plane. Fundus photographs are useful for early screening and detection of main causes of vision loss in the developed world, among which are AMD, glaucoma and Diabetic Retinopathy. The 2-D depiction of the retina obtained by fundus images is lacking the ability to apprehend so much depth, which led to an incorrect diagnosis of some retinal infections [10] . On the other hand, the OCT is a non-invasive imaging procedure which displays informative crosssection images of the retina in ophthalmology clinics. In the assessment and treatment of AMD, OCT is a very useful imaging modality. It helps in revealing region of epithelial thinning of the retinal pigment [11] . It also helps in identifying region of fluid beneath or within the retina and also the retinal pigment epithelium as it gives an in depth view of the retina [9] . This is why a dataset with OCT images was chosen for this study.

text: The dataset that was used to train the proposed model of this study is the Kermany [10] dataset available on Kaggle. Two classes of the dataset that is DRUSEN and CNV (Choroidal Neovascularisation), having 32,931 images were used to classify between dry and wet AMD. The training dataset consist of 23,792 images, 4,199 images for validation dataset, and 4940 images for test dataset. This study used the architecture of ResNet50 convolutional neural networks that have been pre-trained on the ImageNet dataset to classify between dry and wet AMD. The ImageNet dataset is an online dataset having more than one million images and one thousand classes which makes the parameters of the network well estimated. Transfer Learning is a deep learning technique that uses weights of pre-trained CNN model.

text: In this study, a pretrained ResNet50 model without fully connected layer was used. Custom fully connected layers were added and the pretrained model weights except last 3 layers were freeze while training. The final three layers as well as the fully connected layers were the finetuned. The model was trained using Adam optimization algorithm and the learning rate was set to 0.001. Adam algorithms works well with noisy data and it helps to train the model faster with a better performance. A batch size of 64, and an epoch of 20 were used to train the model. The inputs to a layer were standardized using the Batch Normalization layer for each batch size so as to reduce the generalization error and also speed the training. EarlyStopping method of regularization was used to stop the training where the validation loss starts to increase so as to reduce overfitting of the model. ReduceLROnPlateau was used to decrease the learning rate when validation loss has not improved in an epoch. Dropout layer was also added so as to reduce overfitting of the model. The Softmax function was used as the activation function of the fully connected layers and ModelCheckpoint was used to save the weights of the model when the validation loss is minimum.
